slides: So, we have a skeleton. Now let's turn it into a full essay, in thirty-five minutes.
Here's a skeleton for the other side, for the cameras, written as chains. About ten words for each argument, from the thing the task asks about, to the final result.
Paragraph two: the cameras are visible, so offenders expect to be identified, they're afraid of getting caught, and there are fewer offences. Support: traffic-light cameras.
Paragraph three: a second reason, resources, as its own chain. And paragraph four: the opponents' chain, privacy, with its weakest arrow circled.
Each chain is the job of one paragraph. When you write, you paste the chain into the paragraph, with different connectors, so it doesn't sound pasted.
Now, the whole task is thirty-five minutes. Here's a plan we recommend.
Up to ten minutes of planning. Two or three for the opening. About six for each body paragraph. Two for the closing, and two or three for proofreading.
Look at the clock after every paragraph. These are just guidelines. In practice, you'll find your own times, and we'll see how to measure them when we review an essay.
In terms of time, we want to finish the skeleton in no more than eight to ten minutes.
Now, eight to ten minutes is a lot. Why? Because finding the right arguments, the right explanations, the right weakenings... that takes time. It doesn't always jump out at you in the first minute.
And the official guide says the same thing: devote the first minutes to formulating ideas and planning the structure.
Once your skeleton is polished and sits well, the writing itself just goes tick-tock. Faster, easier, and in better language, because now you have time to think about how to word things.
Here's a tip for the writing itself.
When I write, I don't just write the whole paragraph in one go.
I think about the first sentence, the key sentence. I word it in my head as well as I can, and then I write it.
And while I'm writing it, I'm already forming the next sentence in my head. If I want, I rewrite it a little in my head, and then I write it.
And while I'm writing that one, I form the next one.
Why? Because it lets me rewrite and fix a sentence before it's on paper. A clearer thread, better language, and fewer corrections afterwards.
And the full essay from this skeleton? Well, you've already seen it. It's the model camera essay from the two lessons 'What Is Expected of Me', at the start of the course.
Go back and read it again. Now you'll recognise every part. The opening, the two chains pasted into argument paragraphs, the rebuttal at the weakest arrow, and the closing.
Read only its key lines, and you see the whole thread. Position, reason, reason, the other side answered, and the same position at the end.
So how long is that on the answer sheet?
In average handwriting, a full essay like the model essay fills about thirty-five to forty lines.
That's well above the twenty-five-line minimum, and easily below fifty.
And remember to leave a blank line between paragraphs. We'll use it for corrections.
The length came from reasons that were explained... not from padding.
